analysis.one_liner: Lets the government break drug monopolies on brand-name drugs priced above what five peer countries charge.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in January 2019 and died there when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to review the price of every brand-name drug each year and flag any priced above the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. For flagged drugs, the government would cancel the exclusivities and patents that block competition, license the drug openly to any manufacturer, and fast-track generic versions. Drug makers would also have to publicly report their pricing, research, and advertising costs. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees in January 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients taking brand-name drugs — including millions of Americans on expensive medicines for cancer, diabetes, and other conditions — would benefit if the government could end monopolies on drugs priced above what peer countries pay, since generic competition typically pushes prices down sharply. Insurers, employers, and government health programs paying for drugs would also save.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: It requires HHS to review every brand-name drug at least annually against median prices in five reference countries, and any drug priced above that benchmark is deemed 'excessive' automatically.

For drugs found excessively priced, the government-granted monopoly (exclusivity and effectively the patent licensing barrier) ends: HHS must void exclusivities, issue open non-exclusive licenses so any company can make the drug, and speed up review of generic and biosimilar applications within 8 months.
Anyone could petition HHS for a price review of a specific drug, and determinations, petitions, and licenses would be published in a public FDA database.
Manufacturers would have to report prices, R&D spending, advertising, and public subsidies drug by drug, with penalties of up to 1% of a drug's daily gross revenues for failing to report.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose monopoly revenue on any drug found overpriced, and would bear the cost of detailed annual reporting on prices, research spending, and advertising.

drawbacks.text: The international price benchmark could strip monopoly protections from drugs whose US prices reflect higher development or production costs, potentially reducing industry incentives to invest in new medicines.

Giving HHS discretion to void exclusivities and set royalties would concentrate significant pricing power in a federal agency, and generic/biosimilar makers entering under government-compelled licenses could face legal challenges and manufacturing hurdles.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — letting the government open overpriced drugs to generic competition instead of paying or forcing patients to bear inflated prices — is large, since US brand drug prices run well above those in peer countries. The main costs are real: a nonpartisan-style review of every brand drug each year could sometimes strip exclusivity from drugs whose US price is genuinely justified by development costs, potentially discouraging investment in marginal or risky drug development, and generic entry under government-compelled licenses could be challenged in court. On balance, the bill targeted only drugs priced above the median in five peer countries, a high bar that keeps the benefit large relative to the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees and their subcommittees in January 2019, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 10, 2019 and referred to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Judiciary — and to subcommittees on Health and on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, markup, or floor vote took place, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
It attracted 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a chamber where the Democratic majority held 231 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their government-granted monopolies and the ability to charge prices well above what other wealthy countries pay, while American patients continued to bear those prices.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 15 original cosponsors from the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price-setting and patent-breaking proposals of this kind and lobbied against them during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; it never advanced far enough for a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill could strip government-granted exclusivities from any drug priced above the median of five peer countries and force open licensing to generic competitors, hitting the revenue of the highest-priced drugs hardest. It would also expose manufacturers' pricing and R&D finances to public reporting.
The bill creates a new pipeline of open, non-exclusive licenses and 8-month expedited reviews for generics and biosimilars of overpriced brand drugs, expanding their addressable market.
